record.paper_title: Some open problems in low dimensional dynamical systems
record.original_question: Determine whether every triangular billiard has at least one periodic trajectory.

evidence.quote: Problem 22. Do all triangular billiards have some periodic trajectory?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a (nondegenerate) triangle. The billiard flow in $T$ is the dynamical system describing the motion of a point particle moving in straight lines inside $T$ at unit speed and reflecting off the sides of $T$ according to the law of equal angles (the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection); trajectories that hit a vertex are left undefined. A periodic billiard trajectory in $T$ is a nonconstant orbit of this flow that, after finitely many reflections off the interior of the sides, returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Prove or disprove: for every triangle $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, the billiard flow in $T$ admits at least one periodic trajectory.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is classically known to be open in general. Periodic orbits are known to exist for all acute triangles (Fagnano), all right triangles, all rational triangles, and—via a computer-assisted proof of R. E. Schwartz—for all obtuse triangles whose largest angle is at most 100 degrees. The general case (in particular obtuse triangles with largest angle greater than 100 degrees, and irrational triangles) remains open.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Triangular Billiards II: One Hundred Degrees Worth of Periodic Trajectories
status_evidence.snippet: An obtuse triangle whose largest angle is at most 100 degrees has a (stable) periodic billiard path.
status_evidence.claim: Periodic orbits exist for all obtuse triangles with largest angle ≤ 100°.

status_evidence.title: Survey Lecture on Billiards (Schwartz, ICM)
status_evidence.snippet: Whether every triangle has a periodic billiard path remains a well-known open problem; partial results cover acute, right, rational, and obtuse-up-to-100-degree triangles.
status_evidence.claim: The general triangular periodic-orbit problem remains open.
